text: Compute waste eventually gets noticed — someone reviews a cost report and asks why a VM is that size. Storage waste almost never gets that scrutiny, because an unattached disk or an old snapshot doesn't show up on an availability dashboard and doesn't page anyone. It just keeps costing money in near-total silence until someone finally goes looking.

Both major clouds can move or expire data automatically based on age and access pattern, instead of relying on someone to remember. Azure Blob Storage lifecycle management rules act on blob age or last-access time — tier to cool after thirty days, archive after ninety, delete after a year, scoped to a prefix like logs. Amazon S3 Lifecycle rules follow the identical shape through transitions and expiration actions: hot while it's actually read, cooler as it ages, gone once it's past its useful life.

The tier choice has a real retrieval tradeoff, not just a storage-cost one — cool and archive tiers are cheaper to hold data in but slower and sometimes costlier to read back out of. These rules belong on logs, backups, and completed batch outputs, not on data an application reads routinely. Moving that to archive to save money just moves the cost onto a retrieval bill, with a latency hit on top.

Finding orphaned resources is a different kind of problem — a search-and-verify job, not a scheduled policy. The classic candidates are unattached managed disks or EBS volumes left behind after their VM was deleted, old snapshots with no retention policy that outlived the change they were protecting against, and disks from environments that were torn down except for the disks. A single CLI query against unattached disk state or available-status EBS volumes finds all of them at once.

Deleting, unlike tiering or listing, is irreversible, so it earns its own discipline. Confirm a disk is actually orphaned and not mid-migration. Check whether a snapshot exists to satisfy a retention or compliance requirement rather than by accident. Tag candidates and wait a grace period, commonly one to four weeks, before the real delete runs, so a forgotten dependency has time to surface. And route the cleanup through the same change process as any other production change — it doesn't look like a deployment, but deleting the wrong disk carries the same blast radius.

That closes out this chapter: right-sizing gave you the real numbers, commitment discounts and Spot applied them to compute pricing, autoscaling turned the same discipline into an automatic cost lever, and storage lifecycle and cleanup caught the spend that was never actively running at all.
